issues.description: The manuscript repeatedly frames the data as a national probability/general-population sample, but the Methods describe a convenience sample of introductory psychology students from a single university. This is not a minor wording issue: it changes the study's design, target population, likely effect sizes, and the validity of all claims about representativeness.
issues.quote: We recruited participants through the introductory psychology participant pool at Victoria University of Wellington. This study uses data from individuals who participated across five semesters of the project (from 2009 to 2013). Of the 374 participants included in this study, the average age was 19 years at Time 1 (2009; M = 19.42, SD = 2.31) and 68% were female.

issues.description: The claim of national representativeness/generalizability is unsupported and contradicted by the actual sample description. A single-university student pool that is young, majority female, and overwhelmingly Pākehā cannot justify inference to the New Zealand population.
issues.quote: Our research uses a nationally representative sample, meaning that our results are highly generalisable, at least to the New Zealand population.

issues.description: The reported confidence intervals are implausibly narrow for N = 374. For example, r = .21 would not have a 95% CI as narrow as [.18, .23] in a sample of 374, and the mean CI for SDO is also far too tight. This strongly suggests that the table values come from a different dataset/sample, or that the sample size is misreported. Because the table underpins descriptive interpretation, this is a serious internal/statistical inconsistency.

The authors explicitly report that constraining the SDO→environment path equal to the RWA→environment path does not worsen model fit (p = .126), which means they do not have statistical evidence that the paths differ. Nevertheless, they conclude that SDO is a significantly stronger predictor. This is a direct inferential error affecting the paper's central conclusion.
issues.quote: We found that our original model provides comparable fit to the data 2(1) = 2.34, p = .126, but based on the pattern of unstandardized coefficients we interpret SDO as a stronger predictor of change in willingness to sacrifice for the environment than RWA in our sample.

issues.description: Using non-overlapping confidence intervals for two dependent correlations as evidence that one correlation is stronger than the other is not a valid significance test. The two correlations share a common variable and are estimated from the same sample, so a formal test for dependent correlations is required.
issues.quote: Of note here is that the zero-order correlation between SDO and environmentalism was stronger than the correlation for RWA, as indicated by the non-overlapping confidence interval.

issues.description: The manuscript claims to study willingness to change behaviour/make sacrifices for the environment, but the described items assess environmental concern and skepticism about exaggeration. These are related but distinct constructs. Drawing conclusions about behavioral willingness from concern/skepticism items is a construct validity problem.
issues.quote: Our study specifically examines the influence of SDO and RWA on people’s willingness to change their behaviour to protect the environment... Environmentalism was measured as participants’ concern about environmental problems. These items were modelled from Liu and Sibley’s [28] environmental concern scale, "How concerned are you about the current state of the natural environment?" and "To what extent do you think environmental problems have been exaggerated?"

issues.description: The dependent variable is inconsistently described as environmentalism, concern about environmental problems, willingness to sacrifice, and willingness to change behaviour. These are not interchangeable constructs. The inconsistency makes it unclear what was actually modeled and undermines interpretation of the findings.
issues.quote: Environmentalism was measured as participants’ concern about environmental problems... We used path analysis to examine associations between SDO, RWA and willingness to sacrifice for the environment.

issues.description: Longitudinal comparisons and cross-lagged paths assume the constructs are measured comparably across waves. That assumption is especially questionable here because an RWA item was not assessed at Time 2, yet the authors do not report any longitudinal measurement invariance testing or how partial invariance was handled. Apparent change or stability could reflect measurement changes rather than true change.
issues.quote: The item "Some of the best people in our country are those who are challenging our government, criticizing religion, and ignoring the “normal way” things are supposed to be done", was not assessed at time two, but included in all other time points.

issues.description: The analytic sample appears restricted to participants present across all waves, and missing data were handled with listwise deletion. In a five-wave longitudinal study this can induce substantial selection bias unless data are missing completely at random, which is not assessed or justified. Modern SEM practice would typically use FIML or multiple imputation.
issues.quote: This study uses data from individuals who participated across five semesters of the project... Analyses were conducted using listwise deletion.

issues.description: Key information needed to judge longitudinal validity—retention rates, wave-specific sample sizes, attrition patterns, and whether attrition was selective—is omitted from the manuscript and deferred to a website. These details are essential, not optional, for evaluating bias and replicability.
issues.quote: Full details about the sample, including the procedure, retention, and demographics of participants, are available on the NZAVS website.

issues.description: The study uses a standard cross-lagged panel model for highly stable, trait-like constructs (SDO, RWA), but does not separate between-person differences from within-person change. Standard CLPM estimates can be driven by stable between-person confounding and do not cleanly identify within-person temporal effects. This limitation is particularly important because the paper interprets the paths causally.
issues.quote: We tested the reciprocal influences between the constructs with a stationary cross-lagged model where all parameters are set as time-invariant.

issues.description: The manuscript repeatedly treats cross-lagged associations from observational survey data as evidence of causal pathways. Cross-lagged ordering does not by itself establish causality, especially in the presence of unmeasured confounding, measurement error, and possible between-person artifact in standard CLPMs.
issues.quote: These results suggest that there is a causal pathway from ideological attitudes to environmentalism.

issues.description: The authors impose equality constraints across all waves because of substantive interest, but do not report comparing this stationary model against a less constrained alternative. If the cross-lagged relations change over time, the imposed stationarity can bias estimates and mask important temporal heterogeneity.
issues.quote: We imposed this stationary cross-lagged model because we were more interested in the overall and comparative effects of SDO and RWA on changes in environmentalism, and not on whether these effects change during the interval measured.

issues.description: The model is described as a path analysis of three variables across five time points, but the text also refers to constraining residual variance for the same item over time, implying an item-level or latent measurement model. The manuscript does not clearly specify whether indicators were modeled individually, whether latent variables were used, how within-wave covariances were handled, or what estimator was used. This lack of detail prevents proper evaluation and replication.
issues.quote: The model included three variables across five measurement points and was conducted in Mplus (version 7.3 [29])... We also constrained to equality the residual variance for the same item over time, so item 1 in the SDO scale had equal residual variance across all time points.

issues.description: The reported chi-square difference statistic is extraordinarily large relative to the reported sample size and coefficient magnitudes, suggesting a transcription, scaling, or model-comparison reporting error. At minimum, this value needs verification and explanation.
issues.quote: These lagged effects were also statistically different (2(1) = 15,389.13, p < .001), a finding we explore more fully in the Discussion.

issues.description: The model is accepted despite a CFI of .86, which is typically considered below acceptable fit thresholds for SEM. Simply appealing to RMSEA/SRMR while dismissing poor CFI because of complexity is not sufficient without stronger justification, sensitivity analyses, or alternative models.
issues.quote: Overall, model fit was poorer for those indices affected by model complexity (e.g. χ2(2279) = 36511.73, p < .001, CFI = .86), however those less influenced by complexity pointed to good fit (RMSEA = .03, 90% CI [.025, .026], SRMR = .07), therefore the model was accepted.

issues.description: The timing of measurement occasions is ambiguous. The study is described as a five-year analysis, but the sample is said to have participated across five semesters from 2009 to 2013. It is unclear whether waves were annual, semesterly, or otherwise irregular, which matters for interpreting autoregressive and cross-lagged parameters.
issues.quote: This study uses data from individuals who participated across five semesters of the project (from 2009 to 2013).

issues.description: The manuscript attributes both SDO and RWA to social dominance theory, but RWA is not a construct proposed by social dominance theory. This conflates distinct theoretical frameworks (social dominance theory vs. dual-process/authoritarianism models) and can mislead readers about the conceptual basis of the hypotheses.
issues.quote: Sidanius and Pratto’s [1] social dominance theory proposes that SDO and RWA are separate but interrelated, and together predict attitudes towards different social groups.

issues.description: Inferential results for path coefficients report 'SD' alongside B, p, and confidence intervals. For parameter estimates this should almost certainly be the standard error (SE), not the standard deviation. As written, the uncertainty metric is ambiguous and statistically nonstandard.
issues.quote: SDO was a stronger predictor of change in environmental sacrifice (B = -.11, SD = .01, p < .001, 95% CI [-.13, -.09]) than RWA (B = -.02, SD = .01, p = .001, 95% CI [-.05, -.01]).

issues.description: Only the three focal constructs are modeled. Given the strong links of SDO, RWA, and environmental attitudes with variables such as political ideology, socioeconomic status, gender, ethnicity, and contemporaneous economic conditions, omitted-variable bias remains a serious threat. Autoregressive controls do not eliminate confounding.
issues.quote: The model included three variables across five measurement points

issues.description: The manuscript does not make the analysis syntax available during review, limiting reproducibility and preventing reviewers from evaluating the exact model specification and constraints.
issues.quote: A copy of the Mplus syntax used will be available on the NZAVS website upon acceptance of the manuscript.
